units.name: environment
units.role: Adapt the library to the Python/dependency environment it runs in, and report on that environment.
units.description: This part of the code is not about HTTP at all — it is about making the library work correctly wherever it happens to be installed. At import time it figures out which optional helper libraries are present (json vs. simplejson, chardet vs. charset_normalizer), warns the developer if their installed versions of urllib3, chardet/charset_normalizer or cryptography are too old to trust, and patches in an alternate SSL implementation when the standard library's SSL module is missing a needed security feature. It keeps the library's official version number, offers old-style import paths (requests.packages.urllib3, .idna, .chardet) so very old code keeps working, provides a handful of tiny low-level helper functions (turning bytes into native strings, checking if text is plain ASCII, checking if an object looks 'file-like' or a request has been fully built) that many other parts of the library lean on, and can print a diagnostic report of the user's Python/library setup for bug reports.

units.name: primitives
units.role: Provide small, effect-free building blocks (header dict, status-code table, response hooks) the domain layer is built on.
units.description: This is a small toolbox of simple, self-contained pieces that the rest of Requests relies on but that never talk to the network, disk, or clock themselves. It provides a special dictionary that treats HTTP header names as case-insensitive (so 'Content-Type' and 'content-type' are the same key), a ready-made table that translates numeric HTTP status codes like 404 into friendly names like 'not_found' and back, and a tiny mechanism for running any user-supplied 'hook' functions against a Response after a request completes. None of these three pieces know about requests, sessions, cookies, or connections — the higher-level Request/Response objects and Sessions call into them, not the other way around.

entrypoints.plain: A dict whose keys are compared case-insensitively; used for HTTP headers.

entrypoints.name: LookupDict

entrypoints.name: codes
entrypoints.plain: A table mapping HTTP status codes to their common names, e.g. codes.ok == 200.

entrypoints.name: default_hooks
entrypoints.plain: Builds an empty hooks dictionary for a new Request/Session.

entrypoints.name: dispatch_hook
entrypoints.plain: Runs any registered callback functions for a given event (currently just 'response') against a Response.

units.name: exceptions
units.role: Define the vocabulary of everything that can go wrong while making a request.
units.description: This unit defines the complete vocabulary of things that can go wrong while making an HTTP request with Requests: connection failures, timeouts, too many redirects, malformed URLs or headers, bad JSON bodies, SSL problems, and a couple of runtime warnings (about file modes or missing optional dependencies). It contains only class definitions describing these error and warning types, arranged in a small inheritance hierarchy so calling code can catch broad or narrow categories as needed, and it performs no network, file, or other I/O itself. Every other part of the library imports these classes to raise or catch specific failure conditions, and the public package re-exports the most common ones so application code can handle them directly.

units.name: cookies
units.role: Define what a cookie jar means for this library and how cookies move between requests, responses, and sessions.
units.description: This is the part of the library that manages browser-style cookies: small pieces of data a website asks the caller to remember and send back on later requests. It provides a cookie storage container that behaves like both a normal Python dictionary (so callers can write cookies['session_id']) and like Python's built-in cookie-jar type (so it correctly understands domain, path, and expiration rules). It also provides helper functions to build a jar from a plain dictionary, pull cookies out of a server's response into a jar, combine two jars into one, and build the Cookie header to send on an outgoing request. Every other part of the library that needs to remember or send cookies — building requests, following redirects within a session, or handling authentication that resends a request — relies on this piece rather than reimplementing cookie handling itself.

units.name: utils
units.role: HTTP plumbing helpers: file/body inspection, header parsing, proxy resolution, default CA bundle, response encoding.
units.description: This is the library's toolbox of small, reusable helper functions that the HTTP client relies on but that aren't specific to any one feature: guessing the filename for an uploaded file, computing the byte length of an upload body, parsing and formatting the comma/semicolon-separated value lists HTTP headers use, deciding whether a given web address should go through a proxy (by reading proxy-related environment variables and the user's .netrc file), locating the default list of trusted certificates for HTTPS connections, and guessing what text encoding a server's response is written in. It has no opinion about requests or responses as concepts — it does the detail-oriented HTTP plumbing that the domain layer calls into. The tiny certs.py file is included here because its only job is to hand this unit the on-disk location of the default trusted-certificate bundle, and nothing else in the codebase talks to it directly.

units.name: auth
units.role: Define what it means to authenticate an HTTP request: Basic, Proxy, and Digest auth.
units.description: This unit defines how Requests proves a user's identity to a web server or proxy. It provides a common plug-in shape that any authentication scheme follows: given an outgoing request, add whatever headers are needed to prove who you are. Built on that shape are three ready-made schemes: HTTP Basic auth (username/password encoded in a header), HTTP Proxy auth (the same idea, for a proxy server in front of the destination), and HTTP Digest auth, which is more involved because the server first rejects the request with a 401 challenge containing a puzzle (a nonce); this code computes the correct cryptographic response and automatically resends the original request with that response attached.

entrypoints.name: AuthBase
entrypoints.plain: The common shape every authentication scheme follows: a callable that signs a request.

entrypoints.name: HTTPBasicAuth

entrypoints.name: HTTPProxyAuth

entrypoints.name: HTTPDigestAuth
entrypoints.plain: Handles the HTTP Digest auth challenge/response handshake, including resending the request.

threading.local() keeps nonce/nonce-count/challenge state per-thread so a shared HTTPDigestAuth instance is thread-safe.

units.name: request-response-model
units.role: Define what an HTTP request and response ARE, independent of how they get sent.
units.description: This is the part of the library that defines what an HTTP request and an HTTP response actually are, as data, independent of how bytes get sent over a network. A caller builds a simple Request describing their intent (method, url, headers, form data or JSON, files to upload, authentication, cookies); this unit turns that into a PreparedRequest — a fully-formed set of bytes and headers ready to hand to a transport layer, building the query string, encoding the body as JSON or multipart form data, computing Content-Length, attaching cookies, and letting an auth handler sign it. On the way back, this unit's Response object wraps whatever the transport layer received (status code, headers, and a raw byte stream) and offers convenient ways to consume it: reading it as bytes or text, parsing it as JSON, iterating it in chunks or lines, following the 'links' header, and raising an exception when the status code indicates an error. It never opens a network connection itself — it only shapes data going in and consumes a stream it's handed on the way out.

entrypoints.name: Request
entrypoints.plain: Describes a caller's intent: method, url, headers, data, and so on.

entrypoints.name: PreparedRequest

entrypoints.name: PreparedRequest.copy

entrypoints.name: Response

effects.description: Response.iter_content()'s generator reads bytes from an already-open response object handed to it by the transport adapter (self.raw.stream()/self.raw.read()) — it never opens a socket itself.
Response.close() calls self.raw.close()/self.raw.release_conn() to release the underlying pooled connection back to the transport layer.
PreparedRequest._encode_files() calls .read() on caller-supplied file-like objects to build a multipart body; it consumes an already-open file handle but never calls open() itself.

units.name: transport
units.role: Actually open connections and move bytes to and from the server over the network.
units.description: This is the part of the library that talks to the network. It takes a fully-prepared request and a set of settings (proxy address, which SSL certificate to trust, how long to wait before giving up) and hands them to urllib3, a lower-level networking library that establishes TCP and HTTPS connections, reuses them for efficiency, and reads the raw reply. This unit converts whatever raw errors or timeouts urllib3 reports into the friendlier error types the rest of Requests understands, and packages the raw reply into a Response object the rest of the library can use.

entrypoints.name: BaseAdapter
entrypoints.plain: The common shape a transport adapter follows (send/close).

entrypoints.name: HTTPAdapter
entrypoints.plain: The default transport adapter, built on urllib3's connection pooling.

entrypoints.name: HTTPAdapter.send
entrypoints.plain: Sends a prepared request over the network and returns a Response.

entrypoints.name: HTTPAdapter.close
entrypoints.plain: Releases pooled connections held by this adapter.

effects.description: Opens and pools real TCP/TLS connections via urllib3's PoolManager/ProxyManager/SOCKSProxyManager, and sends/reads request and response bytes via conn.urlopen().
Validates that CA-bundle and client cert/key file paths exist (os.path.exists/os.path.isdir) before handing them to urllib3, which opens and reads those files for TLS setup.

units.name: http-client
units.role: Turn a method, URL, and options into a sent request and a Response — once, or repeatedly via a Session.
units.description: This unit is the heart of the library: it takes a caller's request for information (which HTTP method, which URL, and options like headers, cookies, authentication, or a body) and turns it into an actual HTTP conversation with a server, returning the server's answer as a Response. It offers two ways to do this: quick one-off calls (get, post, put, patch, delete, head, options, request) for a single answer, and a reusable Session object for making many calls that share cookies, login credentials, connection pooling, and other settings — the one-off functions simply open a fresh Session for each call and delegate to it, so they are not a separate concept from Session, just a convenience. This unit also owns the rules for following redirects: which status codes trigger one, whether the HTTP method or authentication should change, and how cookies carry over from one hop to the next.

effects.description: Reads REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE and CURL_CA_BUNDLE environment variables to pick a default CA bundle for TLS verification when Session.trust_env is True (sessions.py).
Picks time.perf_counter (win32) or time.time as the preferred clock and uses it to measure Response.elapsed in Session.send.
Session.send()/resolve_redirects() delegate the actual socket/TLS I/O to a mounted adapter's send() method (transport unit); this unit itself performs no raw socket calls, only orchestration.
Session.close()/__exit__ close all mounted adapters, releasing pooled connections; api.request() always does this via a `with Session() as session:` block for each one-off call.

violations_observed.note: auth's HTTPDigestAuth registers handle_401/handle_redirect as response hooks (r.register_hook('response', ...)) rather than being invoked through auth's declared AuthBase.__call__ entrypoint. This works because both units agree on the generic hooks mechanism (primitives.dispatch_hook), so it is a documented extension point rather than reaching into private internals, but it means http-client's runtime behavior after a 401 is driven by callback objects supplied by auth, not by a call http-client itself makes through a listed auth entrypoint.

violations_observed.location: src/requests/__init__.py (warnings.warn(..., RequestsDependencyWarning) and warnings.simplefilter("default", FileModeWarning, ...)) vs. src/requests/exceptions.py:14 (from .compat import JSONDecodeError as CompatJSONDecodeError)
violations_observed.note: This is not a boundary violation but a genuine two-way coupling: environment's package-init logic needs two warning classes from exceptions, while exceptions.JSONDecodeError is itself built on compat's JSONDecodeError (environment). Both edges target real, listed entrypoints, but the two units depend on each other, so they cannot be strictly layered — recorded as a finding rather than resolved by merging, since exceptions is otherwise a clean, effect-free domain vocabulary unit and merging it into environment would blur that.
